subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, April 21, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Sir Henry Drayton.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while there are
very many matters which arise in this House from day to day upon which it is very difficult indeed, almost impossible, to agree, it does seem to me that there is one upon which we should be on common ground, and that is the explanations which we as members of the House of Commons give to this House and consequently to the public in relation to the financial statement submitted by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Those explanations, Mr. Speaker, should be of such a nature as to enable the public to fully grasp the contents of that financial statement-the entries, its purport and its effect. Of course I am very well aware that criticism of a justifiable nature is advantageous, that kind of criticism cannot be denied; but criticism which is founded on inaccuracy or which i3 brought forward purely for partisan reasons has two results: First, the public mind is very much confused; and in the second place, it casts suspicion upon the acts of those officers of the crown who are responsible for the preparation and the presentation of the statement in question. Now you will agree, Sir, and I think all hon. members will agree, that to have any suspicion cast on the officers

The Budget-Mr. Marker
of the crown as regards the preparation and the presentation of the statement in question cannot be advantageous either to the public or to this Dominion as a whole.
In the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, certain assertions have been made which are most unfortunate in their inaccuracies. In other cases the facts have been distorted purely for partisan reasons. As a result the public mind is confused. To-day, to the extent of my ability it will be my effort to remove certain of these inaccuracies, to give a fair explanation as regards this financial statement, and what it means and what it purports to be, and also, to the extent of my ability, likewise to give some explanation of the conditions of the finances of this country.
I will first take up the statement which has been submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance. I will review it, and examine it also, with a certain degree of care. I will attempt to give to the entries which therein appear their proper application; and I will also attempt to show the relations, the reflection and effect, which our railway indebtedness have on the financial statements which have been submitted from time to time to this House and consequently to this country. Now, this is the statement vdiich the Acting Minister of Finance submits as the financial statement for the year ending March 31, 1925, and he states that the revenue for the year amounts to $344,000,000. Then he deals with the expenditure and divides the expenditure under two separate headiigs; the first dealing with the ordinary business of the country, and the second dealing with the business of the country -which is not considered to be ordinary business, namely, the railway advances. Likewise the first part of the statement ;s subdivided under three headings: Ordinary expenditure, capital expenditure and special expenditure. As I have stated the revenue for the year is $344,000,000. Part one deals with the expenditure of the ordinary business of
the Dominion:
Ordinary expenditure	 $ 319,700,000
Balance over ordinary	expenditure	 24,300,000
Capital expenditure	 18,077,000
Balance over	 6,223,000
Special expenditure	 4,400,000
Balance over (after providing for the ordinary business	of	the	country).. ..	1,823,000
Which balances out with the revenue of $344,000,000. Part 2. We then come to that part of the business of the country which is 
not ordinary business, and in that category the Acting Minister of Finance states that he has made railway and other advances- almost entirely railway advances as a matter of fact-to the extent of $19,527,000. As against that he applies the balance over, after dealing with the ordinary affairs of the country, of $1,823,000, and an increase in value of certain assets of $4,000,162, making a total amount to apply as against the railway advances of $5,823,102, and he brings down as an increase in the consolidated debt during the year the sum of $13,703,838. I would like to make clear what that statement purports to be. It purports to be a statement relating to the consolidated debt and the consolidated revenue of the country, and brings down as a result the net increase of the consolidated debt alone. It has not, nor is it intended to have, any connection with the railway indebtedness of the country. That is an entirely separate and distinct matter and has to be taken into consideration separately, althougn it is true it reflects to some extent upon the consolidated fund of the country because the two are to some extent related. But this statement is clearly a statement as regards the consolidated fund of the country alone. That being the case, certain criticisms which have been made in this House with regard to this statement seem to me to be most uncalled for. I intend as a matter of fact to read certain of those criticisms and put them on Hansard, because I will take them up for what they are worth as I proceed with my remarks, and I will show that this statement which has been submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Eobb)-and I will treat with that later on in the course of my remarks-is prepared and is submitted and in precisely and exactly the same way as previous statements have been prepared and submitted to this House from year to year. The first statement which I desire to comment upon is that of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and I am extremely sorry that the hon. member is not in his seat this afternoon. I sent him notice that I proposed to quote his remarks to-day. I will read to the House the criticisms to which I take exception, because they are very germane to the remarks I propose to make. At page 1653 of Hansard of March 30, my hon. friend used these words, referring to this statement:
As a matter of fact, it was a presentation that was hopeless in its confusion and baffling in its inaccuracies.

The Budget-Mr. Marler
This budget I cannot conceive as being other than deliberately designed to deceive the people as to the correct condition of affairs. It is a subtle expedient designed to shield a guilty and moribund government from the just indignation of an awakening public opinion.

It is something to be proud of, especially coming from an ex-minister of the crown. It is not an ordinary member of parliament, mark you, Mr. Speaker, but an
ex-minister of the crown who makes the statement that it is baffling dn its inaccuracies and intended to deceive the public. My right hon. friend says that he subscribes word for word, and letter for letter to that statement.
We will now proceed to another criticism offered by another ex-minister of the crown, the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), whom it is always a delight to hear speak in this House, and who expressed himself in no uncertain terms with regard to the statement in the budget and the subsequent explanations which were given of the budget, and we may put them both together in order to be fair. It is a great delight to hear my hon. friend speak, but on this occasion he must have thought he was speaking in some place where he would not be heard and where his voice would not go all over Canada, where any aspersions cast on a minister of the crown would not be cast on the government officials of the country, because these are the words he used:
Or are we to have a conspiracy of silence, or perhaps what is worse, a tissue of half truths, in dealing with the financial condition of our country ? I am reminded of a remark made by Napoleon when he was referring to a German diplomat: he said. That man lies too much. It is necessary to lie sometimes, but not all the time."
Well, Sir, if these hon. gentlemen, exministers of the crown, take any glory out of a statement of this description, I certainly do not. If hon. members opposite take delight in making statements of that kind and sending them across the country they are welcome to whatever pleasure they derive from such a proceeding but if they think they are rendering their party or the country any service they are, in my opinion, very much mistaken. Aspersions of that nature cast on officers of the crown and members of the government concerning financial statements- not as regards questions of policy, not as regards what has taken place or what is put into such financial statements, but ascribing to their authors the deliberate intention to baffle and deceive-are highly improper and no member of the House is justified in resorting to such criticism unless he is sure that his statements are accurate. As a matter of fact the statements which have been made are not accurate in any particular. I do not wish hon. members to take my word in regard to the accuracy or inaccuracy of the statement I make in the House to-day.

speechtext: That is the peculiar attitude of my hon. friends over there. I do not know the reason for it but it is probably disappointment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Might it be that hope has made my hon. friend change his attitude?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think my hon. friends
over there will some day reach the age when disappointment gives place to humour and anger to tolerance. Now taking up the question of the increase in the consolidated debt, I might give these figures to hon. gentlemen opposite-and perhaps they are very unpalatable indeed-but I want to show the increase in the net consolidated debt with the increase in the railway indebtedness owing to the emission of bonds. Then bringing the two together I wish to compare the three-year period of 1920, 1921 and 1922 with
The Budget-Mr. Marler

the three-year period of 1923, 1924 and 1925. That is what I want to arrive at; that is what I want to put frankly and clearly before the House. I am not trying to hide anything, not trying to deceive anybody. I intend going into a comparison of the guaranteed and of the unguaranteed railway issues and making a comparison of the three years. I think that is the question that my hon. friend from Brandon wants answered. As a step to enable me to do that I first of all have to arrive at what is the increase in the net consolidated debt over a certain period. I want to be abundantly fair to my hon. friends opposite in making this comparison. I want to arrive at the point so that they cannot say that I have made this comparison not gi/ing them credit for demobilization expenditures, not giving them credit for assets which have been written down although they were advances made in cash in the past. I want to give them credit for all that and I want to arrive at the result for the second three-year period by means of expenditure other than demobilization, other than the writing down of these decreases. That is the point I want to arrive at, and I want to be absolutely fair to everybody in that respect. Now these are the
figures:
Net consolidated debt March 31, 1919.. $1,574,531,032 Net consolidated debt March 31, 1922.. 2,422,135,801
Increase in three years	$ 847,004,769

non-active list	 228,115,555

That is the figure I would like hon. gentlemen to bear in mind-the figure regarding expenditure of 256,000,000 odd dollars.
Now take the comparison for the next three year period, that is to say the period for the years 1923, 1924 and 1925:
Net consolidated debt, April 1, 1922.. .. $2,422,135,801 Net consolidated debt, March 31, 1925.. . 2,431,487,113
Total	$	9,351,312

I would like my hon. friends to bear in mind these figures, so that the reflection of the railway indebtedness can be joined up and tied up with this.
[Mr. Marler.l
The amount of increase owing to expenditure then of the first year period was $256,240.115 and the increase due to expenditure outside of demobilization during the second period was $3,060,740.
Now I will continue, so that this question as regards the railways may be brought properly into consideration. I think it is only right, before discussing this question, to take into consideration the fact that this debate has centred to great extent around the question as to whether the railway bond issues, less refunding, should figure in the net con-soliated debt. There is something to be said for that, and there is a great deal to be said against it. In the first place, our railway business is an entirely separate business. It, is operated by a board of directors quite distinct and quite independent. That board of directors report to the president. He reports to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the Minister of Railways is the connecting link between the railways and the people of this country. As we all know the railways have been an extremely expensive matter to finance each year. They come year after year to parliament for a certain amount. These amounts have been advanced either in the way of cash advances, in which case they have appeared in the net consolidated debt, or in the way of loans, mostly guaranteed, but sometimes not guaranteed by the Dominion, in which case they have not appeared in the net consolidated debt. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken this stand-and there is something in the stand which they take-that the amount of money which is indirectly guaranteed should appear in the debt of the country. I do not think it should appear in the net consolidated debt, but I think it should be in a separate account. In other words we should have on one side of the sheet our ordinary business and on the other side of the . sheet our railway business; so that adding the two together we would know each year exactly what the additions to the consolidated debt and to the railway debt of the country . are, the two together making our combined debt. Once that is started it is not a difficult thing to do, because we have the entries relating to our ordinary account, which are quite simple, and we can ascertain from the railway report of last year the amount of the bond1 issue outstanding to the public. All one has to do is to add to the bond issues the amount issued each year and deduct the refunding. The result in total will show what the increase in the railway debt is for that year. As against that railway debt we have

The Budget-Mr. Marler
the railways, of course, for what they are worth. That is something we cannot tell, but we will know by the accounting system what our combined debt will be, and we will have our railway debt on the one side and our consolidated debt on the other side. That would be an extremely simple way of placing the matter before the public. That would show exactly by dividing them as they should be divided,-and I think as they are correctly divided-our railway business entirely separate and apart from, our ordinary business of government, which is an entirely different thing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just on that point, would my hon. friend show the extent to which cash should be advanced to the railways each year, so that the comparison with respect to cash and guarantee could be made from year to year, or would he have all railway financing by guarantee?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not make any difference in the least whether cash is advanced out of the consolidated fund or borrowed. In one case it is borrowed on our direct promise to pay, and in the other case it is borrowed on the promise of the railways to pay and that promise made marketable by reason of our guarantee. There is no difference whether it appears in the consolidated debt or the railway debt. One thing is the same as the other. But if my hon. friend wants more direct answer, I would say that I would very much prefer to see our railways finance themselves and borrow money for their requirements, with the possible exception of paying deficits out of the consolidated revenue, and1 let them borrow for any other requirements on their own account, with our guarantee Of course. That would segregate them and keep them separate, and we would know where we stood each year.	it!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member will admit that it is still the public debt of the Dominion?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not denying it. There is not the slightest question that the railway indebtedness, whether guaranteed or not, is our debt. I do not think there is any way of getting away from it. We have the assets of the railways behind us. The point my hon. friend is suggesting is as to whether or not unguaranteed securities should be considered. I think guaranteed and unguaranteed securities are in the same category. They are all our debts, because we have standing after the securities a large amount of money, about $800,000,000, before which ranks our guaranteed securities and also other prior lien securities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would you add the deficit
of the Canadian National Railways to the ordinary expenses of the country-not the guaranteed loans but the operating deficit and so on?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to make this
mlatter clear in the minds of hon. members. Now let us in the meantime forget all about railway accounts. It is not the operating deficits necessarily; it is cash paid out, and it may be paid out for anything at all. It may be operating deficit or refunding, or a number of things, but I think the idea I have suggested is to keep the account for the ordinary service of the country entirely separate, and any cash paid out of that account for the railways would be put on the other side of the account.
I wish to take up another matter. Around this debate has been centred a great deal the question as to whether these guarantees should be included in the net consolidated debt and that debt correspondingly increased each year, and a great many statements have been made-some extremely extravagant statements-as to the increase each year of the railway indebtedness. I am sorry my hon. friend from West York is not in his seat because I am sure he would discuss the matter with me in his usual courteous and kindly way. The hon. member said the railway indebtedness of the year had increased to the extent of $118,000,000. I do not want to accuse him of saying what he did not intend to say, but I have read his speech with a good deal of care, and I have tried to convince onyself that he did not mean what appears in the report of his speech, because it seemed to me from reading his speech that he meant to say that during the fiscal year the railway indebtedness increased by $118,000,000, and he threw back at the Acting Minister of Finance the statement that he had said it had only increased by the bond issues by about $80,000,000. He asked* where is the discrepancy and what is accountable for it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He took that all back this
morning in committee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did he? In any event,
I think the best thing to do is to put the correction on Hansard, and I do so in the most courteous way, because I think the hon. member for West York simply fell there into an unintentional error. This all arose out of a question which he asked on the 16th March last. He asked:
"What additions were made to the funded and unfunded debt of the Canadian National Railways and affiliated companies. . . . during the calendar year 1924?
The answer given by the Minister of Railways and Canals was as follows:

Mr. Graham:
To the debt to the public	 $ 90,814,026 00
To the debt to the government (including interest)	 28,085,159 35

That answer, as given by the Minister of Railways and Canals, is correct in all respects. The error into which the hon. member for West York fell was this:	He asked for the
calendar year and not the fiscal year. The calendar year is the railway year. The fiscal year starts, as everybody knows, on the first April and terminates on the 31st March. Consequently, to get the increase in the railway fiscal year, you have to deduct entries prior to the first April and to add entries after the 31st December. That will give the increase in the railway debt. I have all these figures written out and if I may have permission, I will jfiace them on Hansard so as to avoid reading a number of figures to hon. gentlemen. If we take the figures furnished by the Department of Railways and Canals, deduct the last bond issue of $50,000,000 which was emitted on the 1st February, 1924, not in the fiscal year 1925, and add the bonds issued after the 31st December, 1924, we shall arrive at precisely the same figure which the Acting Minister of Finance gives in his address. There is not one dollar of difference. It aM balances exactly and correctly. With your permission, Sir, I will place this statement on Hansard so that the actual figures will be there in order to controvert this statement of the hon. member.
The entries to which I refer are as follows:
Total indebtedness as above

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the great difficulty
not arise in attempting to take the figures of one year and apply them to the situation in another? It raises confusion, and in discussing railway accounting it is absolutely impossible to apply it to our fiscal year without misleading somebody.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the Minister of
Railways and Canals for the information. He is absolutely correct in what he says. So difficult, indeed', is it to apply railway finances to our fiscal year without an enormous amount of study, I was almost intending to suggest that the fiscal year and the railway year be made exactly the same so that we would know where we stood. It is a great mistake, with a tremendous business expending tens and hundreds of millions of dollars per annum, not to know where the money is going without having to sit down for many a long night, week after week studying these matters in order to put them before the House intelligently. If the government would consider changing the railway year to correspond with the fiscal year, hon. members would be saved a great deal of time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have to keep the
calendar year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways
and Canals makes a suggestion which I hesitated to make, but which is a very good one. We have all our taxation periods ending on the 31st December now. Our income tax and sales tax comes up as of the 31st December. Practically all companies throughout the country are making their year the calendar year. To compare our statistics with company statistics, or to make any comparisons at all, is almost an impossibility.

The Budget-Mr. Marler
If we had them all in the calendar year- railway year, fiscal year, company year, taxation year, that would save trouble to everybody and be far clearer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would that not also
make it possible for us to have the Auditor General's report more up to date than it is at the present time?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be very glad to
answer that question, but I cannot. I have not very much more to say and I come now to that part of my remarks which, perhaps, is surrounded with more difficulty than anything else. That is the allocation and reflection of the railway bond issues emitted every year on the net consolidated debt of this country. I have spoken about what the various budget speeches disclosed and did not disclose, and it is not necessary to labour that point any more at the present time. I have made it clear, I think, to all hon. members that as regards the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) and the present Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), whatever bonds were emitted were at least set out :n the budget statement year after year. That is not the point in question. The point in question is this, as to how much of those bonds emitted year after year, have to be	added,	using that	argument,
to the net consolidated debt or, if you put it in another way, to the combined debt of the country. In other words, hon. gentlemen have complained that in a certain year we paid out a great deal of money in cash on account of the railways and we charged that in the net consolidated account. Consequently, the deficit was very large. Now, they say, you come along and say to us: We do not intend to pay out cash, but we intend to finance by way of bonds. Consequently your net deficit is very much less or you may have a surplus as the case may be. There is a good deal in that argument and it has to be fairly faced. The question of policy is one which does not make any difference one way or the other in the financial arrangements. Whether the railways are financed by way of cash or by way of bonds, it matters not, all the obligations of the railways are our debts and have to be taken into consideration in some way or another. If $20,000,000 is issued, guaranteed or unguaranteed, in any particular year, that is reflected in the debt of the country, perhaps not for bookkeeping purposes in the consolidated debt, but in the combined debt of the country. We owe that money and we have to pay it. Of course, as against it, we have the assets, if any, purchased by the funds or
proceeds of those particular bonds. Therefore, in the last analysis it does not make any difference whether we pay cash or issue bonds, for practical purposes we have to take into consideration the net result which is obtained.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would it not be fair to the public of Canada if the budget had disclosed that very phase of the question to which the hon. member refers That is the point I raised a moment ago, about the $10,000,000 cash advance last year and $97,000,000 in 1922. The public cannot understand it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
get the point at all. It does not make the slightest bit of difference how the thing is financed. The budget speech could not disclose this aspect in any possible way. The budget year is entirely different from the railway year, and it is utterly impossible for the Minister of Finance to put in his budget speech the railway speech. They are two entirely different things. My hon. friend does not grasp the significance of the situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman likes
to carry a superior demeanour in this House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not propose to accept it even though I am a back-bencher. What I wish to ask the hon. gentleman is this: Would it be too much trouble for the Acting Minister of Finance, in a word or two, to have noted the fact that the cash advance this year is small compared with those of other years, so that the public would know that, although the obligation was still there, it was in a different form? It is not very much, but it is important.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think it would
have caused the Acting Minister of Finance the slightest pain to say that. As a matter of fact he said it in so many words; he said, "I have advanced the railways $18,077,000 and I have issued 'bonds to such and such an extent of which $17,000,000 has been used for refunding purposes." It is all there. But what information does that give to the public, my hon. friend asks. The public will not sit down and study the public accounts; they cannot be expected to. That is the point I make with the government to-day, and I say that if we have a statement such as I have described we shall know exactly where we stand. But the government is not trying in the slightest degree to conceal what has been done from year to year; it says frankly, "This year $18,000,000 has been spent in cash and there has been so much
The Budget-Mr. Marler

in bonds, and last year there was so much in cash and we issued so many bonds." That is all perfectly clear to my hon. friend, I hope.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hesitate to interrupt, but
it is on a point on which there seems to be considerable confusion and difference of opinion as well. I grant at once that when the government guarantees bonds or makes advances in cash to the National railways the debt is increased; there can be no doubt about that. But if that guarantee of bonds or advance in cash to the extent of twenty, thirty or fifty millions is used for capital expenditures, for which there is an asset in the railways, will the hon. member say, as hon. gentlemen opposite contend, that this has a direct influence on the deficit? It adds to the debt, but does it increase the deficit? I say not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not an easy question to answer. I say that it does increase the deficit. The sum of $28,000,000, let us say, is advanced in cash and $25,000,000 in assets acquired, and my hon. friend says that whereas on one side of the ledger you have a debit and on the other side a credit, the one offsets the other and there is a washout and consequently no increase. That would be quite correct if that asset were active. But it is not an active asset.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why is it not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How can my hon. friend
say that $50,000,000 which we have advanced this year is good, and $50,000,000 which was advanced so many years back is bad? We have $800,000,000 advanced to the railways and that $800,000,000 is good or it is bad. But my hon. friend cannot say that because $25,000,000, which is advanced this year is used for a particular extension, he will therefore chop that off and consider it as good and say consequently that there is a corresponding credit entry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When an ordinary business, such as a manufacturing concern, makes an increase in its plant and equipment, will the hon. gentleman say that the management regard that increase as a loss? Because a deficit is a loss in the strict interpretation of the word. If you increase your assets you do not incur a loss; you increase your liabilities, it is true, but you have a corresponding asset. If you build a branch line you incur a debt but you have an asset against that debt.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have nothing at all except an inactive asset. If a business concern adds to its assets it does so only in the hope that the addition will earn money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And that is what the railways are doing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend, who favours public ownership, is extremely hard to convince.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the difficulty with you; you are opposed to it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not opposed to it at all, but I want to see the expenditures of the country lessened and I want to face the situation quite honestly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So do I.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend wants to do that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In a moment. W'hat I say is that the assets of the railways must be considered as non-active assets in our combined debt until it is shown just what they are worth. The assets are there and we do not know what their value is, and we must treat them in the consolidated debt as inactive.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member says that the $800,000,000 consists of inactive assets, he will see that some of that may be a loss; perhaps the whole of it might be a loss. But why segregate any portion of it? On the basis of that argument you might destroy the whole investment of the railways.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

The hon. member is

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

The Budget-Mr. Marler

My hon. friend can take all the comfort he likes out of it. I do not get any comfort out of it, because the 30th April is coming along and my income tax will go into the railway deficit.
Even taking into consideration railway expenditure, we have to take into account to some extent other expenditure also and we have to try if we can,-and I think we canto practise the virtue indicated1 by that hated word " economy ",-hated by every politician from one end of the country to the other- and if possible to do without luxuries, so that taxation can be reduced, because that is after all the only way we can reduce it.
In my remarks to-day I have attempted to give a clear exposition of the financial position in reference to the statement submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance, and to controvert statements from another quarter of the House by members who have been ministers of the crown, and which I think they should not have made.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure
that hon, members of this House and the ordinary people of the country will be delighted with the clear exposition of the financial statement as set forth in the budget. If I were to describe this, I would say that we have to-day listened to a second budget speech. That has not been unusual since this government has come into power. We have had on nearly every occasion two or three budget speeches. The hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Marler) started out this afternoon to make the situation perfectly clear, and he ended up with as much criticism of the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance as ever came from this side of the House. Now, Sir, if we ordinary people have been delighted this afternoon with the differences of opinion as expressed by these giants of finance, principally on the other side of the House, I am in greater confusion that I ever was as to the situation. Two simple questions were submitted to the hon. member to-day, neither one of which he answered. But we had all the assurances in the world that these questions would be answered. One was a simple question, what is the actual deficit to-day-the actual deficit or surplus whichever you like to call it? That question has not been answered. It may be that my poor mental capacity has not been able to grasp it, but I would be very much surprised if any hon. gentleman in this House

has been able to say from the speech of the hon. member for St. La/wrence-St. George what it really is.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Permit me to say
that each time the hon. member speaks he makes confusion worse confounded. We ask him for the deficit of this year, a very simple question. Now he is giving it to us in three-year periods. In other words any hon. member who wishes to know the financial position of the country must take the budget back for years. Why should he stop at three years, four years or five? Why not go back to ten? This is the position in which we ordinary members are placed to-day. We cannot get the deficit for this year. Unfortunately my hon. friend has left the chamber, and I will ask him on some other occasion what the deficit or surplus, whatever he calls it really is, and I will reserve further remarks on this particular point until he is in the chamber.
The budget debate, despised as it is in the press and in the country, brings to us a flood of valuable information from different parts of Canada which we appreciate and which we derive not so much from listening to the speeches as from reading in Hansard the opinions of the different members of the House. It has a peculiar influence on some members. In the case of some members it produces a spirit of prophecy. This mantle was thrown over the shoulders of the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Thurston) the other night. Under the influence of this debate he predicted the absolute dissolution of the party in this section of the House known as the Conservative party. According to his prediction in twenty-five years this party was to

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
be absolutely dissolved. I do not know his reason for such a prediction, but it looks to me more like the whistling of a boy going through the woods, or some dark place, to keep up his courage, or perhaps a funeral had just passed by a short time before and he had to make a noise to divert his thoughts. The hon. member for Victoria had heard of a funeral which had passed some time before. That funeral was the passing of a party to which he claims allegiance in Ontario, known as the Farmers' party. The funeral was a big surprise and occurred in spite of predictions which had been made in regard to the party concerned. In 1920 that party in the Ontario legislature numbered some 45 members, and the Conservative party numbered 25. Predictions were very plentiful in the legislature,-[DOT] and I heard them at the time, being a member of the legislature,-that the old .political parties had now come to the point where they were going to be dissolved and disappear. But unfortunately for those predictions, when the local election of 1923 came about, the party making those predictions was reduced to a baker's dozen, whereas the Conservative party now numbers some seventy-seven members. The hon. gentleman was likely whistling to keep up his courage, because he had, I suppose, looked up the figures in regard to his constituency. For the legislature that constituency is divided into north and south ridings and I would like to show the dissolution which took place after the election of 1923. In 1920 in North Victoria the Rev. Edgar Watson, Progressive member, received 3,348 votes; Robert Mercer Mason, Conservative, 2,430 votes, a majority for the former of 918. In 1923 the Rev. Edgar Watson received 2,353 votes and James Raglan Mark, Conservative, 2,711 votes, or a majority changed over in these two elections in favour of the Conservatives of some 1,270 votes. If we look at the southern part of his constituency, we find that in 1920 Fred George Sandy received 2,542 votes. John W. Wood, Conservative, received 1,103 votes, or a Progressive majority of 1,349. In 1923 Robert J. Patterson, Conservative polled 3,880 votes, Frederick G. Sandy, 3,354 votes and L. V. O'Connor, Liberal, 1,865 votes, leaving a Conservative majority of 526. This was the way in which the Conservative party dissolved, died, disappeared, following predictions such as we have heard here by local members in the legislature. The Conservative party will enjoy a dissolution of that kind, and if the predictions and prophecies continue and produce the 150
same results, we have no complaint with regard to the future.
The budget debate in addition produces some gymnasts. In the last three years we have been amused at the speed with which some members of this House can jump from one part of the House to the other according as the budget pleases them. It has also produced courage in some members. The leader of t'he party to the left (Mr. Forke) has become very courageous thir year. In fact, he says that he has now nailed his colours to the mast. Unfortunately, we who have watched the different budget debates are amused by this great display of courage. One has only to read the statements made by the hon. gentleman in the past, and there are a number to which I would like to draw the attention of hon. members and ask where these colours will be hoisted. It looks to me as though he was sailing in a vessel in which he could change the colours quite' often. In fact, it is very often a vessel with a camouflaged colour, so that one does not know what kind of a vessel it really is. He said:
As regards reduction of taxation we are ready to say amen to it. We will not in any way quarrel with the carrying out of such reductions. Now we are patiently waiting to see what they have done to cut down the expenses of carrying on the business of the country.
Having nailed his colours there, he immediately proceeded to support the government which put upon the people of this country an increase of 100 per cent in the sales tax. Again, speaking of the growing cost of government, he said:
The country demands economy, but I do hope that the economy effected will be a wise economy.
Having hoisted the colours again, he immediately proceeded to support the government in an increase in the cost of civil government of $265,000, an increase in the Immigration department of this country of $680,000, an increase in the Public Works capital expenditure of $1,100,000. Again he nailed his colours to the mast in saying:
We expected the estimates would be cut down very considerably.
And again:
I think it is a mistake that so many supplementary estimates Should be brought down in the dying days of the session.
On each of those occasions the hon. member voted for the government on the very policy for which he condemned them. Therefore, this year when he announces that he has nailed his colours to the mast, we are patiently waiting to see how soon this colour

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
will be taken down and transferred to some other part.
Coming to the financial report as submitted by the minister, like many members of this House, I have for weeks and weeks studied this report in order to get some idea where we stand. I do not wish to go any further than to get an idea of our actual condition year by year. It is not a matter of importance to me what they did ten, twenty, or even six years ago. It is of great importance if we can understand what we, as members, are doing in this House from year to year. It is important if we can grasp just the ordinary figures as given,' to us. While we are not greatly interested whether we have a great or a small surplus, every hon. member is anxious to know whether ordinary expenditure from year to year does at any time equal or surpass ordinary-revenue. As an ordinary member of this House I took the figures as given by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). He gives us the statement that we have derived revenue amounting to $244,000,000; that we have expended $342,177,000, leaving what he calls his actual surplus of $1,823,000.
This is the point where we enter into discussion and we try to ask questions as to whether or not we have this surplus. We have listened to the hon. member who has just concluded and I must say that even now he has not made clear to me whether there is a surplus or whether there is a deficit of some $16,000,000. And why do I say $16,000,000? I give that figure for this reason: having adopted their new policy of giving cash out of the fund, the government gave to the National Railways some $18,000,000, and if that is a cash grant out of our revenues, what other conclusion can we come to than that we have a deficit of $16,000,000? If it is not regarded in that way, then, according to the acting minister, it should go into our debt. But if it is derived from the revenues and taken out of the fund, the minister should explain what the actual cash is; and we as ordinary members cannot figure it in any other way than to apply that to the expenditure of $342,000,000, which would leave a deficit of $16,204,000. The hon. member has laboured all afternoon and has not made that one point clear; and the bone of contention is as to how we shall account for that $18,000,000 given to the railways. If it i3 taken out of the fund it should surely go as ordinary expenditure and so make a deficit of $16,000,000. The next point in the statement refers to the public debt.
